title: Introduction to Web Design
section: 12. Web Design School - Create a Website that People Love
summary: Motivates a design-focused module: users judge a site on looks within seconds, and visual polish can strongly raise perceived value. Previews the four pillars covered next: colour theory, typography, UI design and UX design.

concepts.heading: Why design matters
points: Functionality and clean code are necessary, but users mostly talk about and remember how a site looks and feels, not how bug-free it is.
First impressions form within a few seconds, so a visitor judges the brand, product and company almost immediately, comparable to an interview or a first date.

Case study: a children's juice carton site with clashing colours, mixed typefaces and inconsistent text colours was compared with a redesign by a professional. The redesign used a consistent colour scheme and better font choices.
In the informal survey she cites, people would pay up to about $1 per carton on the messy site versus about $3 on the redesign, roughly a threefold jump in perceived value from design alone.
Design is described as one of the cheapest ways to make a product look premium, and getting reasonably good at it does not require a long learning curve.

concepts.heading: Module roadmap: the four pillars
points: Colour theory: choosing and combining colours so a palette feels consistent.
User interface (UI) design: arranging visual elements to guide attention.
User experience (UX) design: making the whole journey through the site easy and pleasant.
(Extra) These map directly onto CSS skills from earlier sections: colour values, font-family and font properties, spacing and layout, and page structure.

pitfalls: Treating design as an afterthought once the functionality works.
Using many unrelated colours and typefaces on one page, which makes a site look unprofessional.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Design matters': blurb on first impressions. Tasks: 1) restyle a deliberately messy product card with a single colour scheme; 2) limit it to two fonts; 3) align and space the elements consistently; 4) compare before and after.
Starter code idea: a product card with five clashing colours, three fonts and uneven spacing.
Interactive demo idea: a before/after slider showing the messy and cleaned-up versions of the same card.
